findings: B: refuted — “Ett svepskäl är det inte.” and “Så lyder ensemblens invändning, och jag skriver under på den”

C: refuted — “Fler särskilda kvällar begär jag inte. Fyra kan bli sex och sedan åtta, och den som hör dåligt får ändå rätta sig efter någon annans kalender”, plus “Att ensemblen vänjer sig vid remsan kan jag inte lova”
D: refuted — “Om lilla scenen kan bära samma sak vet jag inte” and “något förslag för den scenen har jag inte”
justification: B dies on the four-word sentence “Ett svepskäl är det inte.”, reinforced by the writer signing on to the ensemble's objection. C dies on “Fler särskilda kvällar begär jag inte” and on the refusal to promise the ensemble will get used to the strip — it inverts both halves of §6. Rebuilt D dies on the two clauses in which the writer declines to extend the proposal to the small stage. Key A is carried by “bör texten gå på varje föreställning på stora scenen” together with the conceded cost in §4 (“Kostnaden är verklig” / “Ändå ska den bäras”).

findings: A: refuted — “Slingans symbol finns längst ned på varje uppslag i programbladet” places the symbol in the page footer of every spread, so it is not a mark on that one row; and “Salongen har en hörselslinga” makes the loop a whole-house service on every evening, not a captioned-evening label
B: refuted — same span: what recurs “längst ned på varje uppslag” is the symbol, while the row's own description in §1 is “en egen rad, inklämd mellan syntolkning och skolföreställningar”
C: refuted — “Längre bak i programbladet står Ingegerd Hörnfeldt under rubriken Text och teknik” places the technician elsewhere in the programme
justification: Rebuilt A dies on “varje uppslag” — a mark that appears on every spread cannot distinguish one row — with “Salongen har en hörselslinga” confirming the loop is not what the row announces. B dies on the same sentence read the other way round. C dies on “Längre bak i programbladet” under a separate heading. A and B are two mis-splices of one source sentence, which is a legitimate pattern but does narrow the item's coverage; A is the softer of the pair because its refutation is by relocation rather than verbatim contradiction.

findings: B: refuted — “och mot det hjälper varken broddar eller lättare lass”
C: refuted — “Lassen gick på kälke i stället, och kälken drogs för hand”, with “Hästen fick stå i stallet” as the second span
D: refuted — “Hästen fick stå i stallet” is the only thing the text says about where the horses were during the crust period, and it is the negation of being put to other use
justification: B dies on “varken broddar eller lättare lass”, which names studs explicitly and denies them. C dies on “kälken drogs för hand” — the option borrows the passage's own “i stället” and reattaches it to the wrong agent, which makes it the strongest of the three. Rebuilt D dies on “Hästen fick stå i stallet”; it is the weakest kill in this candidate, since the refutation depends on reading that clause as covering the crust period rather than only the bearing hours, and no span assigns the horses any alternative work. Key A is carried by “Skaren som bar en karl gick sönder under hoven”.

findings: A: refuted — “Var gård körde för sig, och sällan väntade någon in grannen”

C: refuted — “Barnen provar den med hälen som vi gjorde, utan att det ska bli någon färd” sits in the present-day frame and explicitly yields no journey; the working-era test is “Man provar med hälen innan man ger sig ut”, with no children in it
D: refuted — “Vi gick tvärs över sjön mot Olivia Sjödins lada, en väg som inte finns resten av året”, and “räknas varken diken eller gärdsgårdar”
justification: A dies on “Var gård körde för sig”, the exact opposite of taking turns. Rebuilt C dies on the time frame: the children appear only in the “Nu plogas vägarna” paragraph and “utan att det ska bli någon färd” rules them out of any work at all — a well-built trap, the second strongest in the round. D dies on “en väg som inte finns resten av året”. Key B is carried by “Veckorna kom när de kom” and “Man såg på himlen och bestämde sig kvällen innan”.

findings: A: refuted — the count is “how many blows take it to a hundred millimetres” while “The floor is 130 millimetres of washed silica sand”, so the cone was never driven to the bottom
B: refuted — “under a ring weight raised to a collar and let fall” fixes the drop height, which kills “from whatever height each point seemed to need”
D: refuted — exact inversion of “The gap between my February morning and my July afternoon is still wider than the gap between this school and any other school I test”
justification: A dies on 100 mm against a 130 mm bed. B dies on “raised to a collar”, a standardised stop. D dies on Pallenmoor's own comparison, which it reverses term for term. Key C is confirmed by “in the cold the first blow took the cone two-thirds as deep, and the count nearly doubled” read against the 3° morning grid and the 18° afternoon grid.

findings: A: refuted — “the wax he brought up from the bottom was in better condition than the wax at the top”
B: refuted — “The sand itself had hardly changed: the grains he sieved came out much as the original specification had them”
C: refuted — “Eighty millimetres of it had not been turned since the day it was laid, and under nine years of hoofprints it had gone firm enough to lean a spade on”
justification: A dies on the wax being better at the bottom, B on the sieved grains matching specification, C on the untouched 80 mm being firm under nine years of hoofprints — the option asserts loose and out of reach, and the passage asserts firm and under them. Key D is carried by 8 per cent fibre in the top 50 mm against nearer 3 lower down.

findings: A: refuted — “The waxed ones move, whatever their age”, and the comparison set includes arenas “some of them older than this one”, so age is expressly not the variable

C: refuted — those schools are “laid on plain sand and fibre”, i.e. uncoated; the supplier sentence (“the blend on the grains changes from one supplier to the next”) is a caveat on quantifying, not a description of the sprinkler schools
D: refuted — “He has the same pair of grids from a hundred and forty other arenas”, so the hours are held constant
justification: A dies on “whatever their age” plus “older than this one”. Rebuilt C dies on “plain sand and fibre” set against “The waxed ones move” in the next sentence, which classifies the sprinkler schools as having no coating at all — a good trap, because it recycles a real sentence about suppliers from a different argument. D dies on “the same pair of grids”. Key B follows from that contrast plus §3's “The wax is a paraffin blend, and it is doing most of that work.”

findings: B: refuted — the soundness question is left open (“The tester measures a surface; there is no horse above the cone”; “injury records he would trust from hardly any of them”), and §5 reports the yard's changes without any soundness claim, closing on “the thermometer beside them reads four”, below the six-degree threshold

C: refuted — the readings confirm the riders rather than correct them (“hard and slippery for a January lesson, deep and tiring by a July afternoon” is matched by “in the cold the first blow took the cone two-thirds as deep, and the count nearly doubled”); what is corrected is the yard — “The yard has blamed the machine, then the mix, then the man on the tractor”, then “though not in the way the yard had blamed it”

D: refuted — “and it is worth more than they are” reverses the writer's rating; the option's adjective “fuller” is itself textually true (“a good deal less than the trade's brochures offer”), so the whole option turns on the evaluative verb “rates”
justification: B dies on the piece's explicit refusal to answer the soundness question and on the closing image, which leaves the temperature cause untouched (heaters “costed and not ordered”, thermometer at four). Rebuilt C dies on the direction of the correction: the riders are vindicated by the grids, and the yard's three successive blames are what the readings overturn. Rebuilt D dies on “it is worth more than they are”, the writer's rating stated in the same sentence. D is the finest-grained distractor in the round and the weakest kill — a reader who stops at the comma finds “fuller” supported — but it is refuted, and key A (“the care is the most useful thing about him”) is stated twice, so there is no second defensible answer.

findings: A: refuted — the mechanism is named and it is not ice: “Below about six degrees the coating is stiff, the grains lock together, and a hoof breaks the surface”; both readings, three degrees and eighteen, are above freezing, and the effect is already full at three

B: refuted — heating cannot reach the July end of the range, “Above about twenty-five it goes slack”; Pallenmoor also refuses the prediction (“I can't put a number on it; these readings won't carry one”), and the tine-sorted pan is a second, temperature-independent cause
D: refuted — exact inversion of “The temperature is doing more in that room than the tractor is”
justification: Rebuilt A dies on the stated wax mechanism plus the arithmetic that three degrees is above zero, so nothing is freezing. B dies on the upper threshold, which heating cannot address, and on the explicit refusal to put a number on the readings. D dies on the quoted comparison it reverses. Key C is the two causes the piece establishes and that §5 tracks as “changed one thing and left the other alone”: the six- and twenty-five-degree thresholds, and the tines at 50 mm in a 130 mm bed now dropped to 80.

findings: A: refuted — “again there has been no signal” marks a second instance of the same phenomenon, not a consequence of the first; the unanimous start does not cause the unanimous stop
B: refuted — “Rather” needs a correction, and the two sentences agree rather than contrast, as “again” confirms
D: refuted — “Elsewhere” demands a change of place, but “five seconds later” keeps us in the same hall at a later moment
justification: All three die on the single word “again” in “and again there has been no signal”, which fixes the relation as additive and parallel: A imposes consequence, B imposes contrast, D imposes a change of location, and only “Equally” encodes likeness.

findings: A is the key; B “cut”: refuted — “cut in” means to interrupt, the wrong sense for a room that fails to start clapping too
C “fall”: refuted — bare “fall in” means to form ranks; the agreement sense requires “fall in with”, and neither is the applause idiom
D “break”: refuted — “break in” means to interject or interrupt, not to add one's applause
justification: The gap needs the sense “start doing it too”, fixed by the next sentence, “that is why the second pair of hands matters more than the first: it turns a private view into a public event.” B and D both mean interrupt, C means form up, and none of the three can express a room adding its hands to a first clapper's — only “join in” does.

findings: A “transaction”: refuted — a transaction is an exchange of goods or value and does not take an “about how long is decent” complement
C “bargain”: refuted — a result noun; “conducted at speed and without words” requires the process, not the deal struck
D “settlement”: refuted — likewise the outcome a negotiation reaches, and one does not conduct a settlement
justification: All three die on “conducted at speed and without words” together with the “about”-complement: the slot needs a process noun that can be conducted and can be about a question, and the coming-down is described as unfolding in real time (“the sound comes down faster than it went up”). “negotiation” is the only candidate that satisfies both.

findings: A “rehearsed”: refuted — “No one has agreed to anything, there is no conductor to watch” and “not one of the people in it could explain how”; it also leaves “Although” with nothing to concede
B “outspoken”: refuted — the adjective applies to speakers and statements, not to applause given a child, and produces no contrast with “not permitted to run long”
C “brief”: refuted — it collapses the concession into a tautology, since “it is not permitted to run long” says the same thing
justification: The “Although” demands a quality that stands in tension with strict brevity. A is contradicted outright by the essay's central claim that nothing here is arranged in advance; B does not collocate and creates no tension; C makes the sentence say “although it is short, it may not be long.” Only “wholehearted” sets warmth against the four or five seconds that follow.

findings: A “narrowly”: refuted — an adverb of margin, not of manner; a room cannot give applause “narrowly”, and it does not explain the audible difference the next clause reports
C “instinctively”: refuted — “A room asked for a big hand” makes the response prompted, the opposite of instinctive, and §2's self-organising hall is the contrast case
D “eagerly”: refuted — “everybody present can hear that it is not the same sound the recorder player got”, so the applause is audibly lesser, not eager
justification: A dies on collocation and on failing the sentence's second clause. C dies on “asked for”. D dies on the explicit comparison with the recorder player's applause. “dutifully” is the only option that carries both compliance and the absence of warmth that the second clause requires.

findings: B: refuted — “Nothing shows on the ward; the colour comes with the spinning”
C: refuted — “Blood gases have never gone by tube; a porter walks those down”
D: refuted — “The loop runs at the speed it always has”, and the fall in rejects is credited to “Two bins are lined with foam, and rejects are down by about half”
justification: B dies on the sentence that places the visible sign after centrifugation and denies any ward-side sign. C dies on “have never gone by tube”, which inverts the option. D dies twice: the loop speed is unchanged, and the halving is attributed to foam-lined bins. Key A is Ashvenor's own quoted words, “It's the stop at the far end that does it”, set against “Between stations the shocks were tiny.” The new closing sentence, “Nobody has lined the other bins.”, is consistent with “Two bins are lined with foam, and rejects are down by about half” — a partial fix producing a partial reduction — and it neither touches loop speed nor revives any distractor.

findings: A: refuted — “The neighbour's attorney enclosed a tracing of the railway company's deposited plan”, so the plan is precisely what the neighbour brought into the letters

B: refuted — the bank was in active use, “cut from above by one and cleaned from below by the other”, and the laying date is an agreed fact rather than a grievance (“both sides agree the thorn was last laid in 1839”); the quarrel opens in November 1845, a month after the survey
C: refuted — “The previous October a surveyor had chained and pegged the line”, October 1845, before “In November 1845 Ephraim Ruddiforth's attorney claimed the bank”
justification: Rebuilt A dies on the very sentence that says the neighbour's attorney enclosed the tracing. B dies on the maintenance clause and on the 1839 laying being agreed by both sides, six years before a dispute that the chronology ties to the railway instead. C dies on the pluperfect and on “the previous October” preceding November 1845 — an inversion of the sequence the whole item turns on. Key D follows from the landmark identification: the claim runs “from the stone gap down to the lane”, the pegged line runs “from the ash to the culvert”, and §1 places the ash in the stone gap and the culvert under the lane.
